content_units: Ontario Security-Deposit Dispute Snapshot

In Ontario, a landlord generally cannot keep a damage deposit for painting or carpet wear because damage deposits are not permitted under the Residential Tenancies Act. Normal wear and tear is also not chargeable to the tenant. Since there is no signed move-in inspection report, the landlord may have a weaker basis for proving the condition at move-in.
Scenario notes
- Move-out date:   2026-01-31
- Claimed deduction:   CAD 900
- Items claimed:   wall paint   and   carpet wear
- Evidence available:   move-out photos
- Missing evidence:   no signed move-in inspection report
Ontario Tenant Response Checklist
Step   Action   What to Check   Expected Result
1   Review what was actually paid   Confirm whether the landlord is calling it a security/damage deposit, key deposit, or last month's rent   Identify whether the deduction itself may be unlawful
2   Compare claim to Ontario rules   Painting refresh and ordinary carpet wear are usually landlord maintenance, not tenant damage   Separate normal wear and tear from actual damage
3   Organize your evidence   Gather move-out photos, lease, messages, payment records, and any repair discussions   Build a clear timeline and proof file
4   Ask for itemized proof   Request invoices, photos, dates, and explanation of how CAD 900 was calculated   Force the landlord to support the claim with specifics
5   Point out missing move-in evidence   Note that no signed move-in inspection report exists   Undercut unsupported before/after damage claims
6   Send a calm written dispute   State that you dispute unfair deductions and request full return of money by a short deadline   Create a written record and invite resolution
7   Prepare to file if needed   If money is not returned, consider the Landlord and Tenant Board or Small Claims Court depending on the amount and issue framing   Escalate with documentation ready
Documents to Gather Before You Respond
-   Lease agreement
-   Receipt or proof of the deposit/payment
-   Bank or e-transfer records
-   Move-out photos and videos   with dates if available
-   Emails, texts, or chat messages   with the landlord about condition, cleaning, repairs, or move-out
-   Any listing photos or earlier photos   showing the unit condition during tenancy
-   Proof of cleaning   if you hired cleaners or bought supplies
-   Any witness statements   from roommates, movers, or others who saw the condition at move-out
-   The landlord’s deduction notice  , if any
-   Any invoices or estimates   the landlord provided for paint or carpet work
Points that help your position
- No signed move-in inspection report
- Claim appears tied to   paint   and   carpet wear  , which are often treated as normal wear and tear unless there is unusual damage
- Landlord should be able to show   actual damage  , not just routine turnover costs
- A landlord cannot automatically deduct money without legal basis simply because they say repairs are needed
Calm Message to Send the Landlord
Subject: Dispute of Proposed Deposit Deduction
Hello [Landlord Name],
I am writing about the proposed CAD 900 deduction relating to wall paint and carpet wear after my move-out on January 31, 2026.

I dispute this deduction. In Ontario, ordinary wear and tear is not the tenant’s responsibility, and I am not aware of any signed move-in inspection report showing that the unit was in a different condition at the start of the tenancy. I also have photos from move-out documenting the condition of the unit.
Please send me the following in writing:
- an itemized breakdown of the CAD 900 claim
- dated photos showing the alleged damage
- any invoices, receipts, or repair estimates
- an explanation of how the claimed issues go beyond normal wear and tear
Unless you can provide clear evidence of tenant-caused damage beyond ordinary use, I request the full return of the deducted amount within 7 days.
I would prefer to resolve this directly and amicably. If needed, I will rely on my documentation and pursue the appropriate Ontario process to challenge any improper deduction.
Thank you,
[Your Full Name]
[Former Rental Address]
[Phone Number]
[Email Address]
Next Moves if the Landlord Refuses
- Send the message by   email   or another written channel you can save.
- Keep your tone factual; avoid arguing about every minor detail.
- If the landlord does not return the money or provide proof, preserve all records in one folder.
- If the issue concerns an unlawful retained deposit under Ontario tenancy rules, review the   Landlord and Tenant Board   process.
- If the dispute becomes a straightforward money claim outside the Board’s process,   Small Claims Court   may also be relevant.
